client: I've been really stressed since I got laid off from my tech job last month. The bills keep piling up and I just freeze every time I try to update my resume - it feels like nothing I did there was good enough anymore. I'm not sure how talking about this will help when what I really need is another job.
therapist: It sounds like this layoff has really shaken your confidence, especially when you describe freezing up while trying to update your resume. I notice you're speaking very quickly - would you say there's a sense of urgency or pressure you're feeling about the job search right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, there's definitely pressure. I keep seeing my savings go down every month and it freaks me out. But every time I sit down to work on my resume, my mind just blanks and I feel like I'm not good enough for any job out there now. 

It's stupid because I know I have experience, but what if employers see the gap in my work history and just toss my application? That thought makes my chest tighten up.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming this feels - the financial worries mixing with self-doubt makes perfect sense. Your voice sounds quieter and more withdrawn when you talk about the resume, like part of you is shrinking away from the task. What comes up for you when you notice that tightening in your chest?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I just freeze up every time I try to update my resume because it brings up all these thoughts like "Who would even want to hire me?" or "My experience isn't good enough." The chest tightness gets worse when I imagine sending out applications and getting rejected. It feels safer to just avoid the whole thing, even though I know that's not helping.
therapist: Your words sound heavy with doubt, yet your voice has an almost hurried quality - like part of you wants to rush past these painful thoughts. That tension between wanting to move forward but feeling stuck must be exhausting. Would it help to slow down and unpack one of these thoughts at a time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
You're right, I do feel stuck. Part of me wants to just power through these feelings, but another part knows I can't outrun them. It's just...when I slow down, the loneliness and guilt hit even harder, and that scares me. 

I guess one thought that keeps coming up is how I pushed people away when my anxiety was really bad last year. Now I feel like I don't deserve to reach back out to them.
therapist: I hear how painful this isolation feels, especially when you're carrying so much guilt about past relationships. Your voice gets softer and higher when you talk about reaching out - it sounds like that idea brings up some real vulnerability. Would you be willing to explore what "deserving" support might look like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know if I can even answer that question about "deserving" support. Every time I think about reaching out to someone, I just hear this voice in my head saying I don't have the right after how I've acted. It's like...the loneliness hurts, but the idea of bothering people with my problems feels selfish.
therapist: That inner critic sounds particularly harsh when it tells you reaching out would be selfish. I notice your voice speeds up when talking about this - almost like you're trying to quickly explain away your need for connection. What might it feel like to challenge that thought that you'd be "bothering" people?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know... it's not just about challenging the thought. When I imagine texting a friend, my stomach knots up because I can already picture them sighing or making excuses. Maybe they wouldn't say it, but I feel like I'd be adding to their stress. 

It's easier to just stay quiet, even though that makes me feel worse later. The thought of reaching out makes me feel guilty, like I'm being needy or taking up space I don't deserve.
therapist: It sounds like these thoughts about reaching out create such intense physical discomfort that avoidance feels like the only option. I notice your voice becomes more animated when describing these scenarios - almost like you're bracing for rejection before it could even happen. What do you make of that gap between what you imagine others might feel and what they actually say?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client:
It’s true—I always brace for rejection, even when nothing’s happened yet. I guess it’s like my brain assumes the worst-case scenario to protect me, but it ends up making things harder. The gap you mentioned feels huge because I can’t trust my own predictions—what if I’m wrong and they actually do reject me? That’s even scarier.  

I don’t know. It’s hard to believe others might feel differently than I imagine, especially when I’ve been burned before. It feels safer to avoid than to risk being hurt again.
therapist: You've described this protective mechanism so clearly - expecting rejection to avoid being caught off guard, even though it keeps you isolated. I hear both the wisdom in that protective part of you and the loneliness it creates. Would it feel possible to test one small prediction, like reaching out in a low-stakes way, just to gather some actual evidence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying, but even low-stakes reaching out feels terrifying to me. What if they don't respond at all? That would just confirm my worst fears. I've had that happen before and it made me feel even more alone. 

The idea of testing predictions makes sense logically, but my anxiety spikes just thinking about sending a simple text to someone. It's like my brain goes straight to imagining all the ways it could go wrong.
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of reaching out brings up a lot of fear and memories of past disappointments. Your voice speeds up when you talk about this, like your mind is already racing ahead to all the possible negative outcomes. What would it feel like to focus on just one small step instead of the entire interaction?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess you’re right that I’m already thinking about everything that could go wrong. It’s like my brain jumps to the worst-case scenario before I even try. Focusing on one small step sounds easier, but what if I mess up even that? I feel like I’ll just end up embarrassed or rejected again.
therapist: I hear how much fear comes up around even small steps - that worry about messing up feels very real. Your voice softens when you talk about this, like part of you is already bracing for disappointment. What would "messing up" actually look like in this situation? Sometimes our fears feel bigger when they're vague.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Messing up would mean trying to reach out to someone and either getting ignored or getting a cold response. I can already picture them looking at their phone and rolling their eyes before not replying. It's not really vague - I've had it happen enough times before that the fear feels completely justified. 

I know you're probably going to suggest I try anyway, but when I think about doing it, my chest gets tight and I start imagining all the worst possible outcomes. It's not just anxiety - it's based on real experiences.
therapist: You're describing these painful past experiences with such vivid detail - it makes complete sense that reaching out would feel risky. I notice your voice sounds more animated now, almost like part of you is trying to convince me (or yourself) how justified these fears are. That tension between knowing what might help and feeling guarded must be exhausting to carry. What would it feel like to acknowledge both the real hurts from your past AND the possibility that not every interaction has to follow that pattern?
